domain: Safety Engineering / Organizational Learning / Crisis Preparedness
topic_summary: Analysis of how aviation and nuclear industries retain catastrophe-avoidance competence across decades without recurring real disasters, focusing on whether simulation exercises constitute genuine competence-sustaining practice or whether only actual catastrophes maintain the operational kernel. The kernel contest centers on what counts as 'exercise' of the competence: simulated crisis vs. lived crisis.

key_entities: Aviation industry (commercial flight operations with simulator-based training)
Nuclear power industry (reactor operations with emergency drill protocols)
Simulator infrastructure (flight simulators, reactor control room mockups)
Regulatory bodies (FAA, NRC - mandate recurrent training)
Crew Resource Management doctrine (aviation safety framework)
Institutional memory (organizational knowledge retention across personnel turnover)
key_tensions: Simulated crisis vs. lived crisis as competence-sustaining exercise
Regulatory compliance (drill frequency) vs. actual skill retention

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: The shared commitment that catastrophe-avoidance competence must be actively exercised to remain operational, not merely documented or remembered
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Safety engineering consensus grounded in empirical observation of skill decay and organizational learning theory

readings.commitment: Simulated catastrophe constitutes genuine exercise of the competence kernel; fidelity of simulation determines retention effectiveness
readings.authority_grounding: Aviation safety record post-CRM adoption; nuclear industry zero-meltdown record in simulator-trained facilities
readings.expected_structural_delta: Regulatory drill mandates treated as sufficient; competence measured by simulator performance metrics; victim set includes only those harmed by inadequate simulation fidelity

readings.commitment: Only actual catastrophe exercises the competence kernel; simulation is rehearsal but not the thing itself; competence atrophies without real-stakes activation
readings.authority_grounding: Organizational learning theory (Weick, Perrow); tacit knowledge literature; combat vs. training distinction in military doctrine
readings.expected_structural_delta: Simulation recognized as necessary but insufficient; competence assumed to decay covertly; victim set includes all exposed to operators whose competence has not been tested under real stakes

readings.commitment: Simulation exercises procedural competence but not judgment-under-stakes; the kernel has two components with different exercise requirements
readings.authority_grounding: Distinction between technical skill (trainable) and adaptive expertise (requires real-world variability); naturalistic decision-making research
readings.expected_structural_delta: Competence partially retained via simulation (procedures, muscle memory) but judgment/improvisation capacity decays; victim set includes those harmed by failures in the non-simulated component

axiom_contradictions.basis: Simulation_sufficiency holds that high-fidelity simulation IS the exercise that maintains the kernel; lived_catastrophe_necessity holds that simulation is categorically not the exercise, only preparation for it. No single framework can hold both: either simulation counts as exercise or it does not.

axes.primary_observable: Gap between regulatory minimum drill requirements and empirically-derived optimal training intervals

deferred_axes.structural_delta: Drill frequency optimized for compliance not effectiveness
deferred_axes.deferral_reason: Downstream extractive consequence of simulation_sufficiency_reading; captured within that reading's constraint story rather than requiring independent axis

omegas.description: At what fidelity level does simulation transition from 'not exercise' to 'genuine exercise'? If hybrid_decay_reading is correct, this threshold may not exist—procedural fidelity may be achievable while judgment-under-stakes remains untrainable via simulation.

If lived_catastrophe_necessity_reading is correct, what is the optimal catastrophe frequency for competence maintenance without unacceptable harm? This may be an unsolvable constraint: too frequent = unacceptable casualties; too rare = competence decay.

Can the judgment component identified in hybrid_decay_reading be transmitted via apprenticeship/mentorship in zero-catastrophe environments, or does it require personal experience of real stakes? Aviation's CRM success suggests partial transmissibility; nuclear's zero-meltdown record in new facilities is ambiguous evidence.

Institutional_memory_decay identifies erosion of 'why' knowledge. Can this erosion be detected before it causes incidents, or is the incident itself the only reliable signal? If the latter, the system requires periodic small failures to maintain competence—a Piton of deliberate controlled failure.

fracture_scan.notes: No fractures detected. Kernel decomposition into three readings captures the structural contest. Institutional_memory_decay passes independence test as separate observable (organizational vs. individual knowledge). Regulatory_compliance_theater deferred as downstream extractive consequence rather than independent axis.
